paper_metadata.title: Noise-Robust Quantum Generative Models for Distribution Learning and Efficient Data Loading

summary: The paper proposes a noise‑robust hybrid qGAN architecture (EfficientSU2–WGAN‑GP) that learns 6‑qubit discretized probability distributions with Wasserstein distance 0.00271±0.00041 (≈88% improvement over the original RY–CZ qGAN baseline). Using the learned log‑normal distribution as a loader for Quantum Amplitude Estimation on a 10‑qubit circuit, the authors estimate a European call option price of 5.47±0.07 on IBM Boeblingen versus a classical Monte Carlo value of 5.43±0.02, reporting <1% pricing error.

experiments.description: Noise-resilient hybrid qGAN for learning a 2D Gaussian distribution on a 6-qubit discretized grid, benchmarked with QCNN and EfficientSU2 ansätze under WGAN-GP and MMD losses against a classical MLP baseline.

algorithm.variant: hybrid qGAN with WGAN-GP and MMD losses; QCNN and EfficientSU2 generator ansätze
algorithm.convergence_criteria: trained for 500 epochs; plateau criterion defined as generator loss and Wasserstein distance stabilized within ±0.002 for 20 consecutive epochs
algorithm.parameter_initialization: random seeds fixed (seed=42); no explicit parameter distribution reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: target 2D Gaussian discretized on an 8x8 grid (64 bins) mapped to a 6-qubit state; generator outputs measurement probabilities over grid bins
problem_formulation.objective_function: minimize Wasserstein-GP or MMD discrepancy between generated and target discrete probability distributions
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: WGAN-GP gradient penalty; MMD kernel loss; depolarizing noise injected on CX gates

problem_instance.description: Synthetic 2D Gaussian distribution learning on an 8x8 grid

dataset_specification.description: mu=0, Sigma=I2; coords=np.linspace(-2,2,8); normalized over 64 grid bins

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: discretized on 8x8 grid; normalized probability mass function
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: mean±std over 20 independent runs for noiseless results; 5 runs for noisy results; five seeds used in benchmarking protocol; convergence speed measured by plateau criterion

implementation_details.classical_solver: SciPy for Wasserstein and KS metrics; classical MLP baseline
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: SciPy multivariate normal generation; grid discretization; affine normalization for log-normal scaling in related experiment
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Wasserstein distance, KL divergence, KS test, fidelity, t-SNE visualizations

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: WGAN-GP volatile but downward; MMD smooth and stable

speedup_claims.caveats: This is an empirical error reduction, not a runtime speedup.

speedup_claims.conditions: qGAN data loading framework in general
speedup_claims.caveats: Asymptotic claim; not directly benchmarked as runtime scaling in this experiment.

complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(2^n) for exact state preparation; classical Monte Carlo baseline not characterized asymptotically here

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: not reported; experiments limited to 6 qubits (64-bin distribution)
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require substantially larger distributions (many more qubits) and fault‑tolerant circuits to outperform classical GANs for distribution learning.
limiting_factors: classical GAN baselines achieve comparable Wasserstein distance
no demonstrated scaling advantage for generative modeling

notes: hardware.type reported as IBM Q Boeblingen / Qiskit Runtime; experiment itself is run on simulator and verified on IBM hardware, but the extracted experiment focuses on the qGAN training/evaluation setup with noisy simulation and hardware verification.
num_qubits inferred from 8x8 grid (64 bins) explicitly mapped to n=6 qubits.
circuit_depth not explicitly reported for the qGAN generator; only ansatz repetitions (QCNN structure and EfficientSU2 reps=8) are given, so depth is null.

num_variational_params not explicitly stated for the full qGAN experiment; QCNN has 28 parameters and EfficientSU2 about 96 parameters, but the paper does not give a single unified count for the experiment.
Table 1 shows classical MMD‑GAN achieving WS ≈0.0029, essentially matching the best quantum model (0.00271).
Experiments use only a 6‑qubit discretized distribution, so no meaningful scale advantage is demonstrated.

experiments.description: Noise-resilient hybrid qGAN for learning a log-normal distribution and using the learned loader for European call option pricing via quantum amplitude estimation on IBM superconducting hardware.

algorithm.variant: QAE with qGAN-loaded log-normal distribution; EfficientSU2-WGAN-GP and QCNN-WGAN-GP loaders
algorithm.convergence_criteria: trained for 500 epochs; pricing evaluated after qGAN convergence
algorithm.parameter_initialization: random seeds fixed (seed=42); no explicit parameter distribution reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: log-normal asset-return distribution discretized on an 8x8 grid and loaded into a 6-qubit qGAN state; QAE then estimates European call payoff on 10 qubits
problem_formulation.objective_function: estimate European call option price using QAE after learning the underlying log-normal distribution with qGAN
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: qGAN loading with WGAN-GP or MMD; depolarizing noise on CX gates during training

problem_instance.description: European call option pricing with log-normal asset returns

dataset_specification.description: S0=100, K=100, T=1, sigma=0.2, r=0.05; generated from ST=S0 exp((r-sigma^2/2)T + sigma sqrt(T) Z), Z~N(0,1)

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: discretized via affine mapping for efficient data loading; 8x8 grid representation
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: pricing compared against classical Monte Carlo; reported simulator and IBM Boeblingen results; error reduction and shot-scaling shown in Figure 8

implementation_details.classical_solver: classical Monte Carlo baseline; SciPy for metrics
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: QAE pricing estimate compared to classical Monte Carlo; VaR comparison

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: not reported for QAE stage; qGAN loader trained as in exp_1

speedup_claims.conditions: QAE with qGAN-loaded log-normal distribution; epsilon_qae = 0.01
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports a log-log slope of approximately -1.0 for QAE versus -0.5 for Monte Carlo, but this is shown in a figure rather than as a direct runtime benchmark.
Shot-scaling result is reported for simulation, not necessarily wall-clock runtime.
Reported as pricing error reduction; exact error definition is not fully specified.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault‑tolerant QAE with deep coherent circuits and large‑scale state preparation for realistic Monte Carlo workloads.
limiting_factors: QAE only demonstrated on a toy 10‑qubit circuit
pricing error already achievable by classical Monte Carlo
qGAN training performed mostly on simulators
quadratic speedup insufficient once fault‑tolerance overhead is included

notes: The paper explicitly states QAE on 10 qubits for pricing and IBM Boeblingen hardware.
Circuit depth for the QAE pricing circuit is not reported; only the loader ansatz repetitions are given, so depth is null.
The qGAN loader is shared with exp_1; no separate variational parameter count for the combined pricing experiment is reported.
Section 4.5 and Figure 8 claim quadratic Monte Carlo speedup via QAE.
However the experiment uses a very small discretized model and does not outperform classical pricing in practice.
